findings.title: CSRF middleware disabled/commented out
findings.explanation: In sqli/app.py the CSRF middleware is commented out in the middlewares list (line 27: "# csrf_middleware,"). The project does define a csrf_middleware that enforces POST request tokens (sqli/middlewares.py, lines 25-38), but because it is not registered in the Application middlewares the CSRF token checks will not run. This leaves POST endpoints unprotected from CSRF attacks and allows an attacker to cause state-changing requests from a victim's browser if other conditions (authentication via cookies) are met.
findings.remediation: Re-enable and register the csrf_middleware in the application's middleware list so the CSRF checks execute, e.g. add csrf_middleware to the middlewares array in sqli/app.py. Ensure that templates/forms include the CSRF token (csrf_processor is present as a context processor) and that token generation/verification logic is properly tested. Consider also using SameSite cookie attributes to further reduce CSRF risk.

findings.title: Jinja2 autoescape disabled (XSS risk)
findings.explanation: In sqli/app.py the Jinja setup is explicitly configured with autoescape=False (lines 33-35). Disabling Jinja2 autoescaping causes template variables to be rendered without HTML-escaping by default, so any user-controlled content that is rendered in templates can result in reflected or stored XSS. The code makes no other indication that all outputs are manually escaped or that only trusted data is ever rendered, so this configuration is a straightforward XSS risk.
findings.remediation: Enable template autoescaping and only mark trusted content as safe. Concretely, remove autoescape=False or set autoescape=True (or use jinja2.select_autoescape to enable sensible defaults). Audit templates to remove uses of |safe on untrusted data and use explicit escaping (e.g. {{ value | e }}) where necessary. Additionally consider adding a strong Content-Security-Policy to reduce XSS impact.

findings.title: SQL injection via Python string interpolation in query
findings.explanation: The code at lines 41-45 builds an SQL statement by performing Python string interpolation with user data and then executes it without parameters: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}) (line 43) followed by await cur.execute(q) (line 45). Because the 'name' value is embedded into the SQL text by Python before it reaches the DB driver, an attacker-controlled name can inject SQL (for example by including quotes and SQL fragments). The repository already demonstrates a safer pattern elsewhere (get uses parameterized queries at lines 17-20), which indicates this unparameterized construction is a real regression and not mitigated elsewhere in the file.
findings.remediation:
Do not interpolate user-controlled values into SQL strings. Use parameterized queries provided by the DB-API/driver. For example:
q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%s)"
await cur.execute(q, (name,))
If the driver uses named parameters (pyformat), use a mapping: q = "INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)" and await cur.execute(q, {'name': name}). Also validate or limit the length/content of 'name' as an additional defence (e.g., enforce a max length and allowed characters).

findings.title: Weak password hashing (MD5)
findings.explanation: In sqli/dao/user.py the password check compares the stored hash against an MD5 digest of the provided password (line 41: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()). MD5 is cryptographically weak, fast, and used here without a per-user salt or stretching. This makes stored password hashes highly vulnerable to offline brute-force and rainbow-table attacks, risking account compromise and credential reuse attacks.
findings.remediation: Migrate to a modern password hashing algorithm designed for passwords (e.g. Argon2, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with adequate iterations) and include a per-user salt and proper work factor. Use a vetted library such as passlib or argon2-cffi for hashing and verification. Implement a migration strategy: store an algorithm/version prefix for existing hashes, verify on login, and re-hash on successful authentication. Do not use raw MD5 for passwords.

findings.title: Session cookies not HttpOnly (exposed to JavaScript)
findings.explanation: In sqli/middlewares.py the session storage is created with httponly=False (line 20: RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=False)). This will cause session cookies to be set with HttpOnly disabled so client-side JavaScript can read/modify them. If an attacker can run JS in the victim's browser (e.g. via XSS), they can read session cookies and perform session hijacking. While this setting alone does not directly enable an attack, it materially increases risk in the presence of XSS.
findings.remediation: Set httponly=True on the session storage so the session cookie cannot be read by JavaScript. Also consider enforcing secure=True (send cookie only over HTTPS) and setting an appropriate SameSite value (e.g. 'Lax' or 'Strict'). Example: RedisStorage(app['redis'], httponly=True, secure=True, samesite='Lax').

limitations: Static review only: no code was executed, so findings are not proven exploitable at runtime.
Only Python (.py) files are reviewed; tests, virtual environments and build output are excluded.
2 candidate(s) were judged not exploitable by the Reviewer.
